entities.summary:
Neferkasokar is the cartouche name attributed to a pharaoh believed to have ruled during Ancient Egypt's 2nd Dynasty, a period of state consolidation following the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. Although traditionally placed at the close of the 29th century BCE, around 2800 BCE, his historical existence remains largely conjectural. Unlike many other pharaohs whose reigns are attested by contemporary monumental inscriptions or artifacts, no archaeological evidence from his supposed era bears his name. His primary attestation comes from much later king lists and historical accounts, making him a phantom figure whose significance lies more in the historiography of ancient Egypt than in any discernible deeds.

His name, which translates to 'Beautiful is the Ka of Sokar,' appears in vital New Kingdom sources such as the Saqqara King List and the Turin King List, both compiled over a millennium after his supposed reign. The Hellenistic historian Manetho, writing in the 3rd century BCE, also includes a pharaoh with a similar name, Nephercheres, in his *Aegyptiaca*, placing him as the fifth ruler of the 2nd Dynasty and attributing to him a reign of 25 years. This reliance on retrospective records highlights the challenges Egyptologists face in reconstructing the early dynastic period, where gaps in the archaeological record compel scholars to critically evaluate the veracity of later traditional accounts.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Neferkasokar's primary significance lies in his problematic inclusion in later Egyptian king lists, which highlights the challenges of reconstructing early dynastic history and the reliance on traditional, non-contemporary sources. His enigmatic status prompts critical examination of historical record-keeping and succession narratives in ancient Egypt.
